newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba, Vatican to prepare for papal visit.
newsitem.headline: Cuba, Vatican to prepare for papal visit.

text.p: Cuba and the Vatican have agreed to make arrangements for Pope John Paul to visit the communist-ruled island, Vatican Foreign Minister Jean-Louis Tauran said on Tuesday.

Archbishop Tauran said Cuban President Fidel Castro had told him a long-standing Cuban invitation to the pontiff was valid. "We have agreed that soon the relevant arrangements will be made for this pastoral visit to take place," he told reporters at the end of a five-day visit.

Tauran, who met Castro on Monday evening, gave no indication when the pope would visit Cuba. Cuban Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina, asked about a date for the papal visit, told reporters at Havana airport it was premature to discuss the precise timing.
"We're not yet discussing which month," said Robaina, who was seeing Tauran off.

Tauran was the first Vatican foreign minister to be invited to Cuba by the government and he came here at a time of marked improvement in relations between the communist authorities and the Roman Catholic church.

"The so longed-for visit of Pope John Paul II to Cuba would represent a culmination and a new departure point on the road towards normalised relations between the church and the state in Cuba," Tauran said.
Castro is expected to meet the pope if he travels to Rome for a United Nations food summit next month.
Robaina, asked about a possible meeting, said it was not yet possible to confirm if the trip to Rome would take place. The Cuban leader traditionally never announces his travel plans in advance.
Cuba invited the pope to visit at the end of the 1980s but then arrangements were never finalised.

Tauran, who declined to answer questions after making a statement at the airport, noted that there were still areas where the church in Cuba had what he called "needs that have to be appropriately evaluated."
During his visit, Tauran said the church would like a wider public role in Cuba, for example in the role carried out by its charity, Caritas.

But while Tauran talked of problems that still existed between the church and state he did not make any remarks, at least publicly, about Cuba's political system. And he pleased his hosts by reiterating the Vatican's rejection of the long-standing U.S. ecomonic embargo against Havana.
At the airport he thanked authorities for a warm welcome and said discussions had taken place in a "frank and serene" atmosphere.
